 Democrats Seize Control of Congress as Voters Rebuke Trump
 Democrats flipped seven Senate seats, including three in states held by Republicans for decades, and overcame a redistricting effort to capture the House. President Trump told The New York Times that he would accept the election results.
 Published Nov. 3, 2026 Updated Nov. 7, 2026 Share full article

 Latest
 Pinned Reid J. Epstein and Kellen Browning 
 Here’s the latest. 
 Democrats seized control of the Senate and the House as voters delivered a blistering rebuke to President Trump in a midterm rout that reset the balance of power in Washington. The romp stretched from coast to coast, with Democrats flipping seats that had spent decades in Republican hands and taking House districts in corners of the country that had long seemed inaccessible.
 Mr. Trump told The Times in an interview that he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” and was prepared to work with Democrats. “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them,” he said. “We’ll probably work something out.”
 Voters swept out Republican candidates who tethered themselves to Mr. Trump and those who sought a modicum of independence from him. Democrats flipped Senate seats in Maine , Iowa , Kansas , Ohio , North Carolina , South Carolina and even Texas , according to The Associated Press. Many of those states had been longtime conservative strongholds. Republicans had held the Senate seats in Texas and South Carolina for decades. The Kansas seat had been red for nearly a century.
 Senator Susan Collins, a Maine Republican who across 30 years in Washington repeatedly foiled Democratic efforts to unseat her, conceded her race to Troy Jackson, a former state legislator whom Democrats anointed in July after their preferred nominee quit the race in scandal.
 In Texas, James Talarico, a state legislator who became a national fund-raising sensation, toppled Ken Paxton, the scandal-ridden Republican state attorney general whom Mr. Trump elevated to the nomination in the spring.
 “We just took back Texas,” Mr. Talarico said in his victory speech. “We just showed that a politics of division is no match for a politics of love.”
 In South Carolina, Dr. Annie Andrews prevailed over Senator Darline Graham, the sister of the late Senator Lindsey Graham. In Kansas, the Rev. Adam Hamilton stunned Senator Roger Marshall, a one-term Republican.
 And Dr. Abdul El-Sayed prevailed in Michigan even after his Senate campaign was rattled on Sunday when his defeated primary rival, Representative Haley Stevens, endorsed the Republican nominee and drew the scorn of her own party.
 Democrats could still widen their lead in the Senate: Ballots were still being counted in Alaska, where Republicans have complained that a potential spoiler candidate could unfairly siphon votes from their incumbent, and in Mississippi, an unlikely battleground where a couple dozen votes separated the two candidates.
 Democrats also notched major victories in races for governor. In Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman to be elected governor in the country’s history. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa was the first Democrat elected governor since Ann Richards in 1990, by ousting Gov. Greg Abbott, a three-term Republican.
 In another race for governor, Dr. Amy Acton became the first woman elected to lead Ohio, emerging from a vicious campaign that included an ad by her Republican opponent that featured her estranged mother. Sherrod Brown, a Democrat ousted from his seat two years ago, will again represent Ohio in the Senate after flipping a Republican seat.
 The results came in a midterm election that is the first national mandate on Mr. Trump’s second term. They showed what polls have indicated for months — that voters are supremely dissatisfied with Mr. Trump and Republicans who have backed his agenda.
 Democrats flipped House seats across the map. And the redistricting effort Republicans undertook in hopes of protecting their majority failed to yield victories that they intended: Democrats won districts in Florida that Republicans redrew to be favorable for themselves, and a North Carolina seat Democrats flipped was also part of the Republican redistricting effort.
 Democratic candidates have blamed Mr. Trump, and the war he started this year in Iran, for the economic hardships that have driven a current of frustration across the nation. Republicans have focused on portraying their Democratic opponents as extreme on social issues and the economy as they played defense in reliably red states.
 Republicans fended off a significant challenge in a Senate race in Florida: Senator Ashley Moody defeated Angie Nixon, a progressive Democrat, in a tight contest to complete the term of Secretary of State Marco Rubio.
 The last polling places closed at 1 a.m. Eastern on Wednesday, in Alaska, and full results for some races may not be known for days or longer .
 Here’s what else we’re covering:
 A complicated landscape: More than 400 Times reporters, editors, data analysts, video journalists and photographers are covering the midterms, seeking to understand a large country with voters who are complicated — and sometimes contradictory. Read more › 
 Minor disruptions: A technical problem with voting machines in Westchester County, N.Y., outside New York City , led officials there to collect ballots by hand in a competitive House race. In Florida, flooding forced more than 20 polling stations across eight counties to be relocated. In North Carolina, technical problems at several precincts caused minor delays; state election officials said they would delay the release of election results to at least 8:15 p.m. from 7:30 p.m. Read more › 
 Election integrity: Many election officials and Democrats have said they fear that Mr. Trump’s attacks on the integrity of U.S. elections could lead to tensions during voting and baseless challenges to the outcome. The administration has sought to prove that many noncitizens have cast ballots, but few people have been charged with offenses related to voting fraud. Local and state officials say they are well prepared to run a secure election .
 Court rulings: A federal judge has turned down a request by Democratic lawmakers and party organizations to prohibit the Trump administration from coercing states into screening incoming ballots. And the Supreme Court issued what appeared to be an extraordinary rebuke to Mr. Trump, signaling that it was not interested in assisting his efforts to interfere with how states administer elections.

 Kansans elect a Democrat as attorney general, voting out Kris Kobach. 
 Image Chris Mann, a Democrat, has worked as a police officer and prosecutor. Credit... Charlie Riedel/Associated Press Kris W. Kobach, Kansas’ Republican attorney general, helped to make claims of widespread illegal voting a potent political issue years before President Trump became the party’s leader.
 But Mr. Kobach was denied another term by voters, The Associated Press reported on Friday. The result demonstrated both how Kansas and Mr. Kobach’s own trajectory have shifted since he crashed onto the national political landscape more than 20 years ago.
 Chris Mann, a Democrat who has worked as a police officer and prosecutor, defeated Mr. Kobach, marking the first time in 20 years that Kansans have elected a Democrat as attorney general.
 It was a momentous election for Democrats in Kansas and across the country. Adam Hamilton, a Methodist pastor and centrist Democrat, became the first member of his party to win a Senate race in Kansas since the 1930s. He unseated Senator Roger Marshall, a first-term Republican and close ally of President Trump. And in the governor’s race, Cindy Holscher, the Democratic nominee, was leading in a close contest that had not yet been called.
 Mr. Kobach was, in many ways, ahead of his political time. As a law professor and Justice Department official in the 2000s, he pushed for tighter immigration laws . And as Kansas’ secretary of state in the 2010s, he sought and received the authority to prosecute people for illegally voting, making national headlines with the handful of cases he pursued .
 Image Attorney General Kris Kobach, a Republican, helped to make claims of widespread illegal voting a potent political issue years before President Trump became the party’s leader. Credit... Charlie Riedel/Associated Press Though studies have shown that a very small percentage of ballots are cast by noncitizens, Mr. Kobach’s focus on the issue helped to elevate illegal voting as a national issue years before Mr. Trump seized on it during his presidential campaigns. During his first term as president, Mr. Trump tapped Mr. Kobach to lead a panel on voter fraud.
 While Mr. Kobach’s message resonated, his own record was more mixed. A federal judge once found him in contempt of court . And Mr. Kobach lost his campaign for governor in 2018 to Laura Kelly, a Democrat, before losing the Republican primary for Senate in 2020. He returned to statewide office four years ago after narrowly defeating Mr. Mann to win a first term as attorney general .
 As attorney general, Mr. Kobach has defended a state law restricting gender-transition treatments for minors and pushed unsuccessfully for an elected State Supreme Court . His office also prosecuted the Mexican-born mayor of a small Kansas town, who admitted to voting in U.S. elections without being a citizen, in a case that captured the attention of the Trump administration.
 Though Mr. Kobach was once seen as an outlier among Republicans, his views on immigration and voting have become centerpieces of the party’s platform during the Trump era. But in that same period, Republicans’ hold on Kansas has slipped somewhat.
 Republicans continue to win presidential elections in Kansas by large margins, but Ms. Kelly won two terms as governor and the once-conservative suburbs of Kansas City have turned blue, repeatedly electing Representative Sharice Davids, a Democrat, to Congress.

 Cait Conley flips a key N.Y. swing seat for Democrats, ousting Mike Lawler. 
 Image Cait Conley, a Democrat, sought to tie Representative Mike Lawler to President Trump in her campaign to flip New York’s 17th Congressional District, where the president is unpopular. Credit... Dave Sanders for The New York Times Cait Conley, an Army veteran and former national security official in the Biden administration, beat Representative Mike Lawler in a suburban New York swing district, according to The Associated Press , flipping a seat that Democrats had identified as a top target on their path to recapture the House majority.
 Ms. Conley rode a wave of voter dissatisfaction with the policies of President Trump, whose tariffs and war in Iran have contributed to higher prices on gasoline, groceries and other essentials.
 “We started this because we knew that America, the land of promise and opportunity, was on the wrong path,” Ms. Conley said late Tuesday at her election night watch party in Pleasantville. “But we knew, if we came together, if we brought people together, that we could fix it. And tonight we show that this fight wasn’t a partisan fight. This was a patriotic fight.”
 The race, in New York’s 17th Congressional District, was not called until Thursday afternoon, partly because of issues with the processing of ballots in Westchester County . That delayed the counting of tens of thousands of votes.
 But long before the results were official, Ms. Conley’s strong performance in Mr. Lawler’s home base in Rockland County led the congressman to concede.
 Speaking at a banquet hall in a Hilton hotel in Pearl River on Tuesday night, Mr. Lawler said that he had called Ms. Conley to congratulate her and that “when all the votes are counted tomorrow in Westchester, it will be pretty clear.”
 The daughter of a postal worker, Ms. Conley grew up just over the border of the district, which includes the affluent suburbs north of New York City and narrowly favored former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Ms. Conley moved back to run for Congress and talked up her years of military service on the campaign trail, beating two more liberal primary opponents in June .
 Still, her work in the private sector after leaving government became the subject of attacks from Mr. Lawler and outside groups supporting him. They bankrolled television advertisements that portrayed Ms. Conley, a former U.S. Army special operations leader, as a corporate puppet beholden to her former employers.
 Ms. Conley made $328,000 in nearly two years of private-sector work, according to financial disclosure reports, but declined to divulge the specifics of what she did for Hidden Level, an anti-drone-systems company, and for Primer AI, the firm where she consulted, citing nondisclosure agreements.
 The two campaigns and outside groups backing them spent more than $60 million inundating voters with advertising over the course of the campaign, according to AdImpact, an ad tracking firm. About half of that money went to supporting Ms. Conley, with much of it spent on ads attacking Mr. Lawler as a rubber stamp for Mr. Trump. “Mike Lawler votes with Trump 100 percent of the time,” a narrator states in one of the Conley campaign ads. (An analysis by Congressional Quarterly found that in 2025, Mr. Lawler voted yes on bills Mr. Trump approved of 94 percent of the time.)
 A former state legislator, Mr. Lawler shot to fame when he unexpectedly defeated Sean Patrick Maloney , the chairman of the House Democrats’ campaign arm, in 2022. That victory, and his re-election two years later, distinguished Mr. Lawler as a Republican who could win in a resoundingly Democratic state.
 The congressman, who flirted with a run for governor last year, went to great lengths to emphasize his independence. He was a lone Republican voice during negotiations over Mr. Trump’s signature domestic spending bill, conditioning his support for the legislation on raising the cap on the state and local tax, or SALT, deduction . (Ms. Conley had argued that there should be no cap on the deduction, and criticized the fact that the legislation that lowered taxes also cut funding for Medicaid.)
 Mr. Lawler also characterized Ms. Conley as aligned with Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York City and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York, both democratic socialists.
 One exchange during the first debate of the campaign summed up the race’s fault lines. Mr. Lawler called on Ms. Conley to denounce Mr. Mamdani, whom he claimed was encouraging antisemitism.
 “I absolutely call out my party when I believe that it’s wrong,” she said.
 “But you don’t denounce Zohran Mamdani,” Mr. Lawler replied.
 “Have you denounced Donald Trump and the harm that he has caused to our families here in the Hudson Valley?” Ms. Conley said in response.
 The voting problems in Westchester County were the product of human error, officials said, but they nonetheless unsettled voters and poll workers on Tuesday. It turned out that the county had updated its ballots and the software for its ballot-reading machines to add an omitted race in Ardsley, N.Y. — but the software change had been made only in Ardsley, meaning the machines in the rest of the county were unable to read the updated ballots.
 Ballots across the county were deposited into orange bags and delivered to a county Board of Elections facility in Ardsley, where a count, under the supervision of lawyers, began late Wednesday morning.
 At the facility on Wednesday afternoon, a Democratic elections commissioner, Tajian Nelson, declined to give an estimate when reporters asked when the counting would be finished.
 “We’re not even able to begin with the E.T.A.,” she said.
 But she added that, by law, the election results must be certified within 25 days. “So based on that, we have to be certified before we have turkey at the end of the month.”
 Kristi Berner and Wesley Parnell contributed reporting from Westchester County.

 A Democratic prosecutor unseats a 10-term Republican in a Virginia House race. 
 Image Shannon Taylor, a Democrat, drew on her record as a district attorney and ran on an anti-corruption platform. Credit... Win Mcnamee/Getty Images A Democratic prosecutor narrowly toppled Representative Rob Wittman, a Republican first elected in 2007, on Thursday, according to The Associated Press , as a tsunami of voter anger reached his Virginia district.
 Shannon Taylor, the winner, ran on her long record as the top prosecutor in Henrico County, in the Richmond suburbs. She accused Mr. Wittman of having profited from stock trading and from tax breaks that he voted for, centering her campaign on a fight against corruption and entrenched “Washington insiders.” (Mr. Wittman vehemently denied the claims.)
 Mr. Wittman kept the margins close, even as many Republicans in districts that President Trump narrowly won fell by large margins. On the campaign trail, he leaned on his deep familiarity with the district and promoted the investments he had secured during his nearly two decades in office.
 The Democratic establishment viewed Ms. Taylor as a star recruit, and she easily cleared the primary field. During her campaign, she also built on the name recognition she had established during an unsuccessful run for state attorney general in 2025.
 The congressional district, Virginia’s First, stretches from the Richmond suburbs to the so-called Historic Triangle of Jamestown, Yorktown, and Williamsburg, and out to the Tidewater region on the state’s eastern shore.
 Mr. Trump won the district by five percentage points in 2024, but Ms. Taylor’s victory signals it might be moving to the left. In her campaign, Ms. Taylor worked to tie cost-of-living increases to Mr. Trump’s policies.
 Ms. Taylor’s victory came even after a costly redistricting plan meant to benefit her and other Democratic candidates fell through. The state Supreme Court blocked the voter-approved map in May.

 John McGuire, a Virginia Republican, wins re-election to the House. 
 Image Representative John McGuire, Republican of Virginia, defeated a Democratic challenger to keep his seat in the House. Credit... Kenny Holston/The New York Times Representative John McGuire, a Virginia Republican, won re-election to the House, according to The Associated Press , holding a seat for his party that had appeared vulnerable earlier this year.
 Mr. McGuire defeated former Representative Tom Perriello, a Democrat who in 2008 won one term in an earlier version of the district, which stretches from Charlottesville to the state’s border with North Carolina.
 Mr. Perriello entered the race against Mr. McGuire last year, when it appeared Virginia Democrats would redraw the state’s congressional maps to create a district that former Vice President Kamala Harris had carried by three percentage points in 2024.
 But when Virginia courts invalidated the redistricting effort , the lines reverted to the 2024 district that Mr. McGuire won by 15 percentage points and Mr. Trump carried by 12 percentage points. Even in 2025, when Abigail Spanberger, a Democrat, sailed to a double-digit victory for governor, the district went for her Republican opponent by seven percentage points.
 After his term in Congress, Mr. Perriello served in the Obama administration as a diplomat in Africa and then worked for the Open Society Foundations, the philanthropic network funded largely by George Soros. Though he remained in the race after the redistricting reversal, his candidacy did not attract large amounts of spending by supportive outside groups.
 Mr. McGuire will return to Congress for a second term in the House. He was first elected in 2024, emerging after he ousted an incumbent, Representative Bob Good, during a primary campaign that split the MAGA movement . Mr. Good had endorsed Gov. Ron DeSantis of Florida during the 2024 presidential primary campaign, which angered Mr. Trump’s supporters even though Mr. Good was among the most conservative members of the House.

 Data reporter Two traditionally stalwart Democratic groups returned to the party fold these midterms after a dalliance with the G.O.P. in 2024.
 Counties with a Black majority had drifted a little more than a percentage point toward Trump two years ago. But when the dust settled this election night, those places moved nearly 16 percentage points toward Democratic Senate candidates. The Democrats ended up beating their Republican opponents by more than 50 percentage points in some counties.
 Young voters also appear to have come back to the Democratic fold after some signs they were willing to vote Republican. After counties with large numbers of 18- to 34-year-olds swung more than seven percentage points to Mr. Trump in 2024, they swerved left by nearly 23 percentage points this year.

 Reporting from Alaska With Democrats performing so well around the country, the party will be looking at Montana as a big potential missed opportunity. For months, supporters of Seth Bodnar, a well-funded left-leaning independent, and Alani Bankhead, the little-known Democratic nominee, feuded with each other and tried to pressure each other to drop out of the race. In the end, neither did and they split Democratic votes, helping Kurt Alme, the Republican, to an easy victory.
 Nov. 4, 2026, 3:13 a.m. ET Christine Zhang 
 Election data reporter Dan S. Sullivan’s lead in Alaska’s Senate race masks the fact that he is underperforming President Trump’s margins in the 2024 race. Much of the reported vote is from ballots cast on Election Day, which are favorable for Republicans. In the 27 districts that have finished tallying such votes, Sullivan is running behind Trump by an average of 12 percentage points.
 In District 22, which includes North Muldoon, one of the most diverse areas in the state, Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate, leads by nearly 20 percentage points among Election Day voters. Trump carried the same district’s day-of vote by nearly four points in 2024. The remaining votes here will be from early and mail ballots, which are expected to lean toward Peltola.

 Reporting from California It’s after midnight in Los Angeles. While the Associated Press has not yet called the city’s mayoral race, Nithya Raman, the D.S.A.-aligned challenger to Mayor Karen Bass, gave a speech that sounded a lot like a victory address. She told the crowd of supporters, who were buzzing about progressive wins across the country, that she was hopeful. “But I’m also really superstitious,” she said, “so we’re all just gonna be cool, OK?”

 Sarah Trone Garriott defeats Zach Nunn in Iowa, flipping a House seat. 
 Image Sarah Trone Garriott defeated a two-term incumbent. Credit... Thalassa Raasch for The New York Times Sarah Trone Garriott, a Democratic state senator and Lutheran minister, defeated Representative Zach Nunn, Republican of Iowa, according to The Associated Press , flipping a key seat to help her party win control of the House.
 Ms. Trone Garriott’s victory over Mr. Nunn, a two-term incumbent who had closely aligned himself with President Trump, was a major breakthrough for Democrats in a district that Mr. Nunn had won twice. Republicans had invested millions of dollars there to defend one of their most vulnerable incumbents.
 It was also a rebuke of the Trump administration’s economic agenda in a politically divided stretch of central and southern Iowa, where Ms. Trone Garriott had made rising costs, health care cuts and the economic consequences of the war in Iran central to her campaign.
 Throughout the race, Ms. Trone Garriott sought to cast Mr. Nunn as a politician more concerned with protecting the president and his wealthy supporters than with the financial struggles of ordinary Iowans.
 “Families are paying too much for groceries, health care and child care, and people are tired of politicians in Washington who look out for themselves,” she said last month, summarizing her central argument.
 Her victory demonstrated the potency of that message in Iowa’s Third Congressional District, which encompasses Des Moines, its fast-growing suburbs and a broad swath of rural Iowa where Republicans have maintained considerable political strength.
 A former Air Force intelligence officer, Mr. Nunn, 47, had spent much of his time in Congress as a steadfast supporter of Mr. Trump’s agenda. He repeatedly backed legislation that cut federal Medicaid spending, declined to break with the president over his sweeping tariffs and for months supported the war in Iran.
 But as polling showed growing dissatisfaction with the war and its economic consequences, Mr. Nunn sought to distance himself from the administration. In September, after repeatedly rejecting efforts to restrict the president’s military authority, he joined a small group of Republicans who voted to curtail Mr. Trump’s ability to continue waging the war.
 The shift was not enough to save him.
 Ms. Trone Garriott, who had opposed the war, repeatedly tied the military operation to rising gasoline and fertilizer prices, arguing that Iowa families and farmers were paying the price for a conflict Congress had never authorized.
 She also attacked Mr. Nunn’s support for the Republican domestic policy law that reduced Medicaid spending, accusing him of endangering access to health care in rural communities already struggling to keep hospitals and clinics open.
 Ms. Trone Garriott, who defeated a powerful Republican incumbent to win her State Senate seat, held public town halls in all 21 counties of the congressional district, making her accessibility to constituents a central contrast with Mr. Nunn.
 She also proved to be a formidable fund-raiser, bringing in more than $8 million by late October, substantially more than Mr. Nunn’s approximately $6 million. Outside Republican groups poured millions into defending his seat even as some of the party’s most powerful super PACs withdrew support from another vulnerable Iowa incumbent, Representative Mariannette Miller-Meeks.
 Mr. Nunn had demonstrated considerable political staying power, rooted in his popularity beyond the Democratic stronghold of Des Moines. But Ms. Trone Garriott appealed to suburban voters and sought to cut into the large margins Republicans traditionally enjoyed in rural communities.

 Max Miller loses in Ohio after ex-wife’s abuse allegations.

Kenny Holston/The New York Times Representative Max Miller, the Ohio Republican whose campaign was rocked by accusations that he physically abused his ex-wife and young daughter, lost his re-election bid, according to The Associated Press , handing Democrats a seat in deep-red territory as they won House control.
 Brian Poindexter , a union ironworker, defeated Mr. Miller, a two-term congressman whose political rise was fueled by his close relationship with President Trump, in a district Mr. Trump won by a double-digit margin two years ago. Mr. Miller had rejected calls by fellow Republicans to drop out of the race after he was accused by his ex-wife, Emily Moreno, of domestic abuse against her and their 2-year-old daughter.
 Image “I never got in this race to run because Max Miller is terrible in his personal life,” Mr. Poindexter said in an interview. “I got in it to run because of policies that hurt us.” Credit... Daniel Lozada for The New York Times Ms. Moreno, the daughter of Senator Bernie Moreno, also an Ohio Republican, said that Mr. Miller had scalded her chest and stomach by throwing hot water from a skillet at her body; held a gun to her head; pushed her against a wall and hit her head; and fractured their daughter’s collarbone and bruised her shoulder. The allegations came to light as part of a lengthy divorce court battle.
 Mr. Miller denied all of the accusations and embarked on a defiant media tour in which he accused his ex-wife of being mentally unstable, a liar, a stalker and a dangerous individual.
 As the sordid family drama gained national attention, some powerful Ohio Republicans, including Senator Jon Husted, pressed Mr. Miller to exit the race and resign. Mr. Moreno, who at first tried to avoid questions about Mr. Miller, eventually said that his former son-in-law was not fit to hold public office.
 “If there are any basic standards of character required to hold elected office, Max Miller fails them,” Mr. Moreno said in an emotional statement. The House Ethics Committee also opened a review of the domestic abuse allegations.
 Some White House officials wanted Mr. Miller to drop out of the race in time for Republicans to replace him on the ballot, but the president stopped short of asking Mr. Miller to drop out .
 In a private phone call, Mr. Trump simply warned him that it might be difficult for him to win given the allegations. Mr. Miller was resolute that he would do what the president himself had done when faced with personal scandals seen as fatal to his presidential campaigns: stay in and fight.
 Mr. Poindexter continued to work full time as an apprentice instructor throughout his primary campaign. He tried to make his own relatable life story part of his pitch to win over working-class Trump voters.
 “I never got in this race to run because Max Miller is terrible in his personal life,” he said in an interview . “I got in it to run because of policies that hurt us.”
 Despite the accusations, Mr. Miller was never fully deserted by House Republican leaders. Once it became clear there was no way to replace him on the ballot, they quietly spent more than $5 million to defend his seat, according to the ad-tracking service AdImpact.

Paul Sancya/Associated Press Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson won the race for governor in Michigan on Wednesday, according to The Associated Press , keeping in Democratic hands an office that has an important role in certifying the closely divided state’s presidential election results.
 Ms. Benson, 49, will take over in January from Gov. Gretchen Whitmer, a Democrat who was barred by term limits from running again, and who built a national profile during eight years in Lansing. Ms. Benson defeated Representative John James, a Republican from suburban Detroit who had lost two previous statewide campaigns.
 Both candidates made an anti-incumbent case to an electorate frustrated by the high cost of living and rising prices.
 While Mr. James blamed the Democrats in state government, Ms. Benson criticized President Trump’s policies, including tariffs targeting Canada that have had an outsized effect on Michigan’s auto industry. She pledged to seek “sub-national” agreements with Canada, which borders Michigan, if elected.
 “At a time where it feels like, at the federal level, government is showing up everywhere we don’t want it and nowhere where we actually need it, I will make sure that government is showing up for you and doing right by you,” Ms. Benson said in a recent debate hosted by WDIV-TV.
 Ms. Benson, a former law school dean who served two terms as Michigan’s chief elections officer, became a target of right-wing activists in 2020 when she presided over Joseph R. Biden Jr.’s victory in the state over Mr. Trump. Ms. Benson defended the results against unproven claims of widespread fraud. After Mr. Trump returned to office, she fought his administration’s efforts to obtain private voter data.
 Michigan’s governor signs a document certifying the state’s presidential electors, a role that could again become important if the results of a future presidential race are contested. Mr. Trump carried the state in 2016 and 2024, while Mr. Biden won it in 2020.
 Ms. Benson will become the first Democratic governor of Michigan to succeed a fellow Democrat since the 1960s. She will also be the third woman to serve as the state’s leader.
 The governor’s race had initially been expected to be a three-way contest including Mike Duggan, a former mayor of Detroit and longtime Democrat who was running as an independent. Though he received significant endorsements and had competitive polling numbers, Mr. Duggan dropped out of the race in May , saying he did not want to be a spoiler. His decision to withdraw was widely seen as a boost for Democrats.

Kenny Holston/The New York Times “America is back,” declared Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, on Tuesday night as Democrats were on the path to a resounding victory in the House. “Today begins the great American comeback.”
 Mr. Jeffries, who is set to make history in January as the first Black speaker of the House, promised a room of ebullient supporters and volunteers in the nation’s capital that Democrats understood they had been given a mandate to deliver “dramatic change.”
 His message to voters: “We hear you. We see you. We feel you. House Democrats are committed to making life better for you,” he said. “This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic one.”
 Mr. Jeffries promised that House Democrats would work on two tracks: to make life more affordable for Americans and to bring accountability to the corruption that the Trump administration has visited upon the country.
 “We’re going to fight for small-town America,” he said. “We’re going to fight for urban America. We’re going to fight for suburban America. We’re going fight for the heartland of America. We’re going to fight for Black and brown communities all across America.”
 Mr. Jeffries, a reserved politician who grew up in a working-class home in the Crown Heights section of Brooklyn in the 1980s, ended on a note of hometown pride.
 “We made it, Brooklyn,” he said. “We made it.”
